title: Lesson 16: Data Safety: What Employees Can and Cannot Put in Tools
description: Grounded in Lesson 16 of the AI Adoption series: why everything put into an AI tool leaves the building, the four-level data classification, PII and data retention, and the three-question decision routine before pasting.

questions.question: Lesson 16 states that the single most important fact about an AI tool is that whatever an employee puts into it leaves the building and may be stored, retained, or used to train the model. Which class of data should an employee default to treating as NOT safe to paste into a tool?
options: Public data such as a published portfolio piece or press release
Internal Only data after the employee removes direct identifiers and shortens the excerpt
Confidential or Restricted data, unless an approved tool and an approved path make the specific use safe
Any data, because tools never retain or train on user inputs
questions.explanation: Lesson 16's three-question routine says that when data is Confidential or Restricted, the default answer is no unless an approved, configured enterprise tool makes the specific use safe. It also cautions that 'I deleted the chat' is not a control because vendors may retain a copy. Public and carefully trimmed Internal Only data may go into an approved tool.

questions.question: Lesson 16 uses the four-level data classification model. Which pair of data types maps correctly to the Confidential and Restricted levels, respectively?
options: Confidential: employee handbooks. Restricted: marketing materials.
Confidential: customer records, contracts, and financial records. Restricted: trade secrets, source code, and active M&A documents.
Confidential: press releases. Restricted: standard operating procedures.
Confidential and Restricted are the same level and mean public information
questions.explanation: Lesson 16 defines Confidential as customer records, employee personal information, contracts, financial records, legal documents, partner agreements, and sensitive business plans. Restricted is the most sensitive tier: trade secrets, source code, intellectual property, board materials, active M&A documents, and regulated personal information.

questions.question: The Samsung case in Lesson 16 illustrates a central point about data safety. What happened, and what did the organization do in response?
options: Engineers pasted source code and meeting notes into a chatbot, which retained the input and led to three separate leaks of corporate information before Samsung restricted generative AI use
Engineers refused to use AI tools, so the company missed a productivity opportunity
The vendor immediately deleted all inputs and no data left Samsung's systems
Samsung recorded the incident internally but took no action and saw no leaks
questions.explanation: Lesson 16 documents the March 2023 Samsung incident from the AI Incident Database: engineers leaked sensitive source code and internal meeting notes by using a chatbot, the chatbot retained the input, and Samsung identified at least three incidents of leaked corporate information before it restricted generative AI use. The lesson uses it to show that a helpful tool can permanently remove data from your control.
